title: Beyond The Label: What The HHS AI Roadmap Means For Healthcare
summary: The US Department of Health and Human Services released its Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap, which outlines an ambitious vision for AI that delivers better answers, faster care, and lower costs.
body_markdown:
The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has released its


[Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/clinical-si-roadmap.pdf) (the roadmap uses the Trump administration’s


[new terminology for AI](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/09/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-inaugurates-the-era-of-super-intelligence/) : “super intelligence”). The roadmap outlines an ambitious vision for AI that delivers better answers, faster care, and lower costs. The vision goes beyond automating tasks: HHS wants safe, reliable AI to support patients between visits and help clinicians focus their expertise where it matters most for each patient.


Per this new roadmap, the US federal government is moving to connect innovation, evidence, regulation, and payment as


[intelligent healthcare organizations](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/investing-for-impact-the-power-of-clinical-intelligence/) and orchestrated platforms take shape and gain momentum. At the US state level,


[AI sandboxes](https://www.forrester.com/report/predictions-2027-healthcare/RES202220) provide supervised environments to test clinical AI, manage risks, and share lessons. Healthcare organizations (HCOs) should prepare now for the transition to intelligent organizations and orchestrated platforms but should not confuse policy ambition with implementation readiness.


### **Four Priorities For Clinical AI**


The roadmap acts as a framework for HCOs to follow, bringing together existing HHS initiatives and planned actions against a backdrop of growing constraints for both


[access and affordability](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-healthcare-plan-that-still-needs-a-plan/) . The administration is positioning clinical AI as another means of addressing these challenges. The direction is promising, but how well the industry implements the roadmap and coordinates innovation, evidence, regulation, and payment will determine whether


[consumers](https://www.forrester.com/report/drive-business-value-with-a-healthcare-ai-value-framework/RES204266) and clinicians benefit and whether HCOs realize


[measurable AI value](https://www.forrester.com/report/drive-business-value-with-a-healthcare-ai-value-framework/RES204266) .


The HHS Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap focuses on four priorities. The roadmap specifies the following:


- **Earn public trust.** Protect patient choice, consent, and control. Build confidence through transparent evidence, staged deployment, and continuous monitoring, weighing AI risks against shortcomings in today’s care.


- **Build the data foundation** **.** Improve secure access to connected health records so patients, clinicians, and AI tools can use relevant information while safeguarding privacy and cybersecurity.


- **Establish clear rules of the road.** Advance risk-based regulation, clarify liability, and pursue national standards. Partner with US states on sandboxes to test clinical AI with appropriate oversight.


- **Pay for what works.** Expand outcome-based payments, including


[ACCESS](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/innovation/innovation-models/access) , and explore Medicaid models with states. Reward improved health and lower costs rather than more visits or technology use.


### **What To Do Next**


The roadmap sets a federal framework for clinical AI, but HCOs must still define their own path forward. When asked about their top concerns in


[Forrester’s State Of AI Survey, 2026](https://www.forrester.com/data-and-insights/surveys/forresters-state-of-ai-survey-2026/SUS197087) , US AI decision-makers in healthcare, pharma, and medical devices organizations cited security, privacy, and compliance (30%), risk management (21%), and governance strategy (21%). But when we asked them about what is included in their leadership-approved AI and agentic strategies,


[fewer than half](https://www.forrester.com/data-and-insights/surveys/forresters-state-of-ai-survey-2026/SUS197087) of these same decision-makers included AI principles and values, technology, talent strategy, or governance strategy. What this means: HCOs have uneven strategic foundations — not simply different priorities. HCOs have not yet clearly defined their AI risk tolerance, the value that AI must deliver, and who is accountable for approving its use, managing its risks, and measuring its outcomes.


To lay the foundations for becoming intelligent healthcare organizations supported by orchestrated platforms, HCO leaders should:


- **Define the strategy, then scale across the organization.** Clinical, operational, digital, and workforce leaders need cross-functional working sessions to align on AI principles, permitted uses, business objectives, and decision rights. Document those agreements and then use onboarding and practical AI use case examples to make explicit to employees and partners which uses are permitted and who can approve them.


- **Set safeguards for AI use and assign ownership.** Establish rules for sensitive data, vendor access, consent, and human escalation. Then, designate a risk lead to map each AI use case to safeguards and a named owner. Assign owners for risk reviews, ongoing monitoring, and incident response, and update safeguards as evidence and regulation evolve.


- **Build governance into how work gets done** **.** Involve frontline staff in workflow design and provide role-based training to challenge outputs and handle exceptions. Accountability must be usable in everyday work, not simply codified in a policy document.


- **Measure value consistently.** Use a


[healthcare AI value framework](https://www.forrester.com/report/drive-business-value-with-a-healthcare-ai-value-framework/RES204266) to connect investments to revenue, efficiency, or risk mitigation. Track access, safety, workforce capacity, and care journeys, and then use those results to decide what scales.
